title: Queries
hook: Quakers ask themselves regular questions about truth, peace, simplicity, equality

segments.voice: Yesterday, meeting for worship: Friends waiting on God in silence. Your line was expectant waiting. Where did you wait today without reaching for your phone? Day one thousand one hundred sixty-six.

Do I keep my word? Read a question like that aloud to a room of Friends, and then leave it there. Not a question about doctrine. A question about the people in the room. The silence holds it. Nobody raises a hand. Nobody is graded. Each person carries it inward and answers it there, or doesn't yet. Friends call these questions queries. Quaker meetings keep written sets of them, about truth, peace, simplicity and equality, and come back to them again and again. Today's word: queries.

Why questions instead of rules? A rule tells you what to do and lets you stop thinking once you've done it. A question keeps working on you. Friends use queries to search their own lives, not to check off a list. It's an old instinct in the Bible. Paul writes to the Corinthians: "Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves." And Lamentations says: "Let us search and try our ways, and turn again to the LORD." Queries gather around what Friends call testimonies, the shape their faith takes in daily life. Truth: Jesus said, "let your communication be, Yea, yea; Nay, nay," and Friends have tried to let a plain word be enough, without oaths. Peace: a query might ask how you meet conflict. Simplicity: what you're carrying that you don't need. Equality: how you treat people, all of them. That last one has a root. George Fox, an early Quaker preacher, urged Friends to "walk cheerfully over the world, answering that of God in every one." That's today's line. Friends speak of that of God as a light in each person. To answer to it is to speak and act toward that light in them, even when the rest of the person is hard going. So a query on equality isn't really about manners. It's about whether you see that of God across the table. A query isn't a test with a right answer. If you answer one quickly, it probably hasn't done its work yet.

Here's the practice: let one question sit with you. Settle your breath. Four themes: truth, peace, simplicity, equality. Choose one. Turn it into a plain question about your own week. Where did I bend the truth? Where did I stir up trouble? What am I holding that I don't need? Whom did I treat as less? Don't rush to answer. Let the question do the work. If you pray, you can hold it before God. If you don't, simply hold it honestly. The bell holds the time.
Queries. Questions Quakers ask themselves in meeting, about truth, peace, simplicity and equality, answered inwardly and never graded.
Your line: answer to that of god. Today, with one person who's hard to like, look for that of God in them, and speak to it. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-six.

notes: Editor pass: hook now opens on the query itself, not a second silent-meeting scene after day 1165; 'long tried' softened; 'wrote from prison' cut (context unverified); 'Friends believe' changed to 'Friends speak of'.
Fox quotation: confirm the exact wording against a standard edition of the Journal (the 1656 letter from Launceston); the context ('wrote from prison') should also be checked.
'Friends have long tried to let a plain word be enough, without oaths' is a general historical claim (Quaker refusal of oaths); confirm or soften.

Example questions in the hook and practice ('do I keep my word?', 'where did I bend the truth?') are illustrative, written in the spirit of the queries, not quoted from any Faith and Practice. Confirm acceptable.
'That of God is the light Friends believe is in each person' — Friends vary in how they speak of the Inward Light; confirm phrasing.
Testimonies named as in the index (truth, peace, simplicity, equality); some Friends add community and integrity.
